questions.prompt: What is the key risk of a 'silent break' when a quantum SDK updates versions?
options: The old API is removed and raises an ImportError immediately
The API still runs without error but changes numerical behavior, with no error to alert you
The package fails to install at all
The documentation disappears
questions.explain: A silent break is dangerous precisely because the code keeps running without any error -- a changed default (like a transpiler setting) can alter numerical output with nothing to flag the change, unlike a loud break which fails immediately and visibly.
questions.distractorExplain: An ImportError describes a loud break, which is comparatively safe because it's impossible to miss -- the silent break is the one that slips past unnoticed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: modern Python packaging uses a ________ file (rather than the older setup.py) to declare a package's metadata, dependencies, and build system.
questions.explain: pyproject.toml is the modern standard configuration file for Python packages, replacing setup.py, and is where quantum SDK versions should be exactly pinned per Lesson 3.

questions.prompt: Select every reason the course gives for why quantum code needs stricter dependency pinning than typical classical Python code.
options: Quantum SDKs like Qiskit have gone through disruptive major version transitions that removed and renamed core APIs
A changed transpiler default can silently alter numerical results between SDK versions
Quantum code cannot be installed with pip
Pinning is only a stylistic convention with no practical consequence for quantum code
questions.explain: The course specifically cites Qiskit's disruptive version transitions and the risk of silent numerical changes (e.g. transpiler defaults) as concrete reasons quantum SDKs need tighter, exact pinning than many classical libraries require.

questions.prompt: A project needs both Qiskit and Microsoft's Q#/QDK toolchain. Why does the course recommend separate virtual environments rather than installing both into one?
options: Q# and Qiskit have independent release cadences and dependency trees not designed to coexist cleanly in a single process
Python forbids importing more than one quantum SDK per file
Separate environments make circuits execute faster on real hardware
Q# cannot be installed on the same operating system as Qiskit
questions.explain: Q#/QDK uses a fundamentally different toolchain (.NET-based) with its own dependency ecosystem and release cadence, incompatible with sharing a single environment alongside Qiskit -- isolation avoids dependency conflicts, not a performance concern.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a quantum function's docstring should state which backend and SDK version its claimed behavior was actually '________ against', not just describe the parameters and return value.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 argues quantum docstrings need a 'Validated against' field recording the specific backend/SDK version a function's expected behavior was actually confirmed on -- information a standard classical docstring template omits.

questions.prompt: Why can't `assert counts == {'0': 512, '1': 512}` be used to test that a Hadamard gate produces a fair coin flip?
options: Measurement outcomes are a random sample, so even correct code will almost never produce an exact 512/512 split on a given run
Qiskit does not allow comparing dictionaries
Hadamard gates never produce the '1' outcome
assertEqual-style tests are banned in all quantum test suites
questions.explain: Because measurement is probabilistic, exact-equality assertions on sampled counts will fail almost every time even on perfectly correct code -- a statistical test with a calculated tolerance is needed instead.

questions.prompt: A Hadamard-based circuit run for 1024 shots returns 480 counts of '0' (expected p0=0.5). The computed z-score is -2.0. Select every true statement about this result.
options: The result fails at 95% confidence (|z| < 1.96)
The result passes at 99% confidence (|z| < 2.58)
The z-score would be different if the shot count were quadrupled to 4096 while keeping the same 46.875% observed proportion
The z-score of -2.0 is independent of the shot count used
questions.explain: z=-2.0 fails the 1.96 threshold but passes the 2.58 threshold, demonstrating why the confidence level must be stated explicitly. Standard error scales with 1/sqrt(n), so quadrupling shots at the same proportion would change the z-score -- it is NOT independent of shot count.

questions.prompt: A statistical test for a Bell state fails intermittently on code that hasn't changed. What does the course say this most likely indicates?
options: The tolerance is too tight for the shot count being used -- a test design issue to fix deliberately
The quantum backend is permanently broken and should be replaced
The test should simply be re-run until it passes, since intermittent failure is expected and meaningless
Construction tests are no longer necessary once a statistical test exists
questions.explain: The course explicitly argues that re-running until it passes is backwards; intermittent failure on unchanged correct code points to a tolerance/shot-count mismatch, fixable by loosening the confidence threshold or increasing shots.

questions.prompt: What does a statevector simulator return that makes it useful for isolating a circuit's logic bugs from sampling noise?
options: Exact amplitudes with zero sampling noise, rather than sampled measurement counts
A random sample of possible outcomes, same as a shot-based simulator
Only the final measured bitstring, discarding all amplitude information
A visual plot of the circuit diagram
questions.explain: A statevector simulator computes exact quantum amplitudes directly, with no sampling involved at all -- so a mismatch there proves the bug is in the circuit's logic, not an artifact of random sampling.
questions.distractorExplain: A shot-based simulator returns a random sample of outcomes, which is exactly the source of noise a statevector check is meant to eliminate from the debugging picture.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: two statevectors that differ only by a ________ phase are physically indistinguishable by any measurement, so comparing them should use Statevector.equiv() rather than raw equality.
questions.explain: A global phase factor (like -1 or i) applied to an entire statevector has no effect on measurement outcomes. Statevector.equiv() correctly treats such statevectors as equivalent, unlike direct equality comparison.

questions.prompt: What problem occurs when a function builds a circuit AND calls backend.run() in the same function body?
options: The circuit's construction logic cannot be unit-tested without also instantiating and running a backend
Python raises a SyntaxError for mixing construction and execution
The circuit will always produce incorrect results
It becomes impossible to ever change the shot count
questions.explain: When construction and execution are fused, there is no way to test just the circuit's structure without triggering an actual backend run -- defeating the purpose of a fast, deterministic construction test.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the backend-abstraction pattern (an abstract QuantumBackend interface with run() and name() methods).
options: It lets the same algorithm code run against a local simulator or real hardware by only changing which concrete backend object is passed in
It should include every capability any backend has, such as get_calibration_data(), so 'all backends have it'
It is a direct payoff of separating circuit construction from execution (dependency injection)
Hardware-specific capabilities like queue position belong in a separate, optional interface rather than the shared one
questions.explain: The pattern enables swapping backends via a single parameter, builds directly on dependency injection, and deliberately keeps hardware-only capabilities out of the shared interface to avoid capability leakage -- forcing something like get_calibration_data() into the shared contract is exactly the mistake the course warns against.

questions.prompt: Why does the course recommend a subprocess-based SDK-adapter pattern (rather than direct in-process import) for combining Qiskit and Q# in one project?
options: Q#'s QDK toolchain and Qiskit's Python ecosystem are not designed to coexist in a single process, so the subprocess boundary keeps their dependency trees isolated
Subprocess calls are always faster than direct function calls
Direct imports of Q# are illegal under its open-source license
Qiskit automatically forbids importing any other SDK in the same file
questions.explain: The subprocess boundary deliberately avoids mixing Q#'s and Qiskit's dependency trees in one process, directly implementing the environment isolation recommended for SDKs that can't coexist cleanly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: passing a backend into a function as a parameter, rather than having the function construct or import it internally, is called dependency ________.
questions.explain: Dependency injection is the pattern of supplying a dependency like a backend from outside a function, which is what makes the backend-abstraction pattern and multi-backend testing possible.

questions.prompt: A team builds a full multi-SDK adapter layer for a project that has never needed and has no concrete plan to use a second SDK. What does the course call this?
options: Speculative abstraction, generally worth avoiding until a second SDK is an actual, current requirement
A required best practice for every quantum project regardless of scope
The backend-abstraction pattern working as intended
A necessary step before any construction tests can be written
questions.explain: The course explicitly warns against building the SDK-adapter layer before there's an actual current need for multi-SDK support -- adding that complexity speculatively is an over-engineering mistake, not a best practice.

questions.prompt: What does the course mean by a 'traceable' experimental result?
options: A result that can be mapped back to the exact git commit, pinned dependency environment, and random seed/shot count that produced it
A result that was printed to the console at least once
A result obtained only from real quantum hardware
A result with more than 1000 shots
questions.explain: Traceability requires all three pieces together: the exact commit (via a git tag), the exact resolved environment (via a lockfile), and the exact run-time parameters (seeds, shots, backend version) -- missing any one breaks full reproducibility.

questions.prompt: Select every item the course says must be recorded together to make a quantum experiment's result fully reproducible later.
options: A git tag identifying the exact commit
A lockfile capturing the full resolved dependency environment
The random seeds used (simulator seed, transpiler seed, and any optimizer seed) and the shot count
The researcher's personal opinion of how the experiment felt to run
questions.explain: The course ties together three jointly necessary pieces -- the git tag (code), the lockfile (environment), and the recorded seeds/shots/backend version (run-time parameters) -- as what reproducibility actually requires; subjective impressions play no role.

questions.prompt: Why does pinning `qiskit==1.2.4` in pyproject.toml alone not guarantee full environment reproducibility, according to the course?
options: Because qiskit's own transitive dependencies (like rustworkx or symengine) can still resolve to different versions across machines without a committed lockfile capturing the entire resolved tree
Because pyproject.toml files cannot specify exact versions with ==
Because qiskit version numbers are not globally unique
Because pinning only applies to test dependencies, never to qiskit itself
questions.explain: An exact pin on the direct dependency doesn't fix the versions of its own transitive dependencies. A full lockfile (uv.lock or a pip freeze snapshot) is needed to capture the complete resolved environment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: for real-hardware experiments, the course recommends recording a calibration ________ instead of a random seed, since physical hardware noise reflects the device's current error-rate state rather than seeded pseudorandomness.
questions.explain: Real hardware noise isn't seeded the way a simulator's randomness is -- it reflects the device's calibration state at the time, which drifts over time, so the course recommends recording the calibration timestamp instead of a seed for hardware runs.

questions.prompt: A previously pinned SDK version becomes uninstallable years later. What does the course say you should do?
options: Document that exact reproduction is no longer possible, re-run under the closest installable version, and report it as a new, separately tagged experiment
Silently substitute the new version's result for the old one under the same experiment tag
Delete the original result permanently since it's unverifiable
Refuse to ever upgrade any dependency in the project again
questions.explain: The course explicitly warns against silently substituting results. Instead, document the limitation honestly, re-run under a new version, and tag that as a distinct new experiment -- any discrepancy is itself worth investigating, not hiding.

questions.prompt: Why is applying Python's cProfile to a `backend.run()` call against real cloud hardware close to useless?
options: Most of that time is queue wait and network latency outside your own code, so cProfile faithfully reports 'waiting' without anything actionable
cProfile cannot be imported in any quantum project
Real hardware calls execute too quickly to be measured
cProfile only works with classical, non-numeric Python code
questions.explain: cProfile profiles time spent inside your own code's execution. Queue wait for a real-hardware job happens outside your process entirely, so cProfile has nothing useful to attribute it to.

questions.prompt: For Grover's search over N=1024 items, using the formula (pi/4)*sqrt(N), the number of oracle iterations needed rounds to ____.
questions.explain: (pi/4) * sqrt(1024) = (pi/4) * 32 ≈ 25.13, which rounds to 25 -- verified by direct computation and used as a regression-locked test value in the capstone.

questions.prompt: A QAOA circuit has p=3 layers (6 parameters). Using the parameter-shift rule over 100 optimizer iterations at 2000 shots per circuit evaluation, what is the total shot budget for the full training run?
options: 12,000 shots
2,000 shots
600,000 shots
questions.explain: evals_per_gradient = 6 params * 2 = 12; total_executions = 12 * 100 = 1,200; total_shots = 1,200 * 2,000 = 2,400,000 -- verified by direct computation, illustrating why a full training run costs far more than a single circuit's shot count suggests.

questions.prompt: A planned real-hardware VQE/QAOA run is projected to need roughly 5x more shots than the allocated budget. Select every adjustment the course identifies as a genuine option, each with its own real trade-off.
options: Reduce optimizer iterations, risking the optimizer not converging
Reduce shots per evaluation, increasing standard error and potentially destabilizing convergence
Train on a local simulator and reserve real hardware only for a final validation run
Ignore the budget and submit the full run anyway, assuming the queue will sort itself out
questions.explain: The course presents three concrete, calculable adjustments -- each with a real trade-off except the simulator-training option, which avoids trading away convergence or precision entirely. Ignoring the budget and hoping it works out is not a strategy the course endorses.

questions.prompt: Why does the course recommend checking a circuit's required qubit count against a backend's actual qubit count as part of resource estimation, before submission?
options: A circuit needing more qubits than the backend provides fails trivially, and catching this before submission avoids wasting queue time on a job that can never succeed
Qubit count has no bearing on whether a circuit can run
Backends automatically expand their qubit count to match any submitted circuit
This check is only relevant for classical programs, not quantum ones
questions.explain: This is the most basic feasibility check in resource estimation -- a circuit that needs more qubits than a backend has cannot run at all, and discovering this from an error message after submission wastes queue time that could have been avoided.

questions.prompt: Why does the capstone library deliberately scope to only three well-understood algorithms rather than many novel ones?
options: Because the goal is demonstrating depth of software-engineering discipline per algorithm, not breadth of algorithmic coverage or novelty
Because implementing more than three quantum algorithms is technically impossible
Because quantum algorithms cannot be tested in groups
Because the course ran out of lessons to cover more algorithms
questions.explain: The capstone explicitly prioritizes exercising every chapter's engineering practice in depth on a small, well-understood algorithm set, rather than maximizing algorithm count or novelty.

questions.prompt: Select every requirement the capstone's requirements document ties to a specific earlier lesson as a checkable acceptance criterion.
options: Circuit construction separated from execution (Lesson 10)
A statevector test confirming exact entangled-state structure (Lesson 8)
A statistical test with an explicit, documented confidence level (Lesson 7)
A requirement that the code 'feels well-tested' without further specification
questions.explain: The capstone's requirements document deliberately avoids vague criteria like 'feels well-tested' in favor of specific, lesson-referenced, checkable requirements -- separated construction/execution, a statevector check, and a documented-confidence statistical test are all real examples from the document.

questions.prompt: In the capstone's final code review, why is a missing experiment-record workflow for reported results treated differently from a missing QAOA statevector check?
options: The statevector check is a genuine acknowledged gap needing future work, while experiment records aren't a gap at all since no experimental results have actually been reported yet to apply that workflow to
Both are treated as equally severe failures with no distinction
Experiment records are more important, so the statevector check is ignored entirely
Neither is considered relevant to the final review
questions.explain: The review distinguishes a genuine, acknowledged gap (QAOA lacks a statevector check it should eventually have) from something that isn't actually missing in context (Chapter 4's experiment-record workflow exists for reported results, and none have been reported yet in this capstone).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an explicit, honest '________ limitations' section in a project's documentation is considered far more trustworthy than a silent gap a user discovers themselves later.
questions.explain: A 'Known limitations' section states explicitly what hasn't been validated or built yet, letting users calibrate trust accurately -- the capstone-level version of the same honesty principle applied to docstrings in Lesson 4 and Lesson 23.

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson the capstone's final wrap-up draws about carrying this course's practices forward into real quantum projects?
options: Tiered testing, backend abstraction, pinned dependencies, experiment records, pre-submission resource estimation, and honest documentation all apply identically to real quantum research code and production software at any scale
These practices only matter for small, educational capstone projects and don't generalize to real work
Real quantum projects should skip testing since hardware noise makes tests unreliable anyway
Only the architecture patterns from Chapter 3 are relevant beyond this course; the rest were just exercises
questions.explain: The course's closing point is that every practice built across all six chapters generalizes directly to real quantum research and production code at any scale -- the capstone was intentionally small so the practices, not the algorithm count, would be what's actually learned.
